comparison: Both evaluate cadherin expression patterns (C20-C23). OpenEval finds claims well-supported by immunofluorescence, RNA-seq, and ELISA data. Peer reviewers agree, with Reviewer 3 calling data 'very high quality and convincing.' Peer R1 also covers P-cadherin null phenotype (C24-C26), which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.
OpenEval R2 evaluates P-cadherin null phenotype (C24-C26) as supported. Peer R1 covers these same claims alongside cadherin expression patterns, with no challenges raised by any reviewer.

Both address E-cadherin loss consequences (C27-C34). OpenEval finds multiple lines of evidence support AJ disruption and P-cadherin upregulation. Peer R2 confirms 'E-cadherin is important for maintaining adherens junctions, tight junctions, and integrity of the niche.' Peer R2 also covers tight junctions (C38-C39) and desmosomes (C40-C42), which OpenEval addresses in R5 and R6.

OpenEval R4 evaluates F-actin disruption claims (C35-C37) as supported by phalloidin staining. Peer R2 broadly confirms structural consequences of E-cadherin loss but does not specifically detail F-actin findings.

OpenEval R5 addresses tight junction disruption (C38-C39) with immunofluorescence and barrier assay data. Peer R2 confirms tight junction effects as part of broader structural findings but does not detail the functional barrier breach data.
OpenEval R6 evaluates desmosome maintenance (C40-C42) as supported by EM and immunofluorescence. Peer R2 notes niche integrity findings but does not specifically discuss desmosomal compensation.

Both address ectopic proliferation in telogen bulge (C43-C45). OpenEval finds EdU data clearly support the claims. Peer R3 calls this a 'fascinating observation that hair follicle stem cells can sense the barrier breach and engage in a hyper-proliferative state without triggering hair follicle growth.'

Both evaluate bulge hyperthickening and stem cell expansion (C46-C49). OpenEval finds histology, immunofluorescence, and quantification support the claims. Peer R3 confirms findings are 'strongly supported by the data' and highlights the repurposing of proliferation.
OpenEval R9 addresses return to quiescence in subsequent cycles (C50-C51). Peer R3 broadly accepts proliferation dynamics but does not specifically detail the return to quiescence observation.

Both evaluate genetic controls showing niche dependence (C52-C54). OpenEval finds P-cadherin overexpression and stem cell-specific ablation controls support that niche perturbations drive proliferation. Peer R4 explicitly confirms 'Ablation of Cdh1 specifically in bulge stem cells did not cause the stem cell proliferation phenotype indicating that niche signaling is responsible.'

Both address P-cadherin overexpression control (C52). OpenEval includes this in broader genetic dissection. Peer R17 specifically notes this control is not questioned and supports that P-cadherin upregulation alone does not drive proliferation.

Both evaluate temporal and niche-specific ablation experiments (C55-C57). OpenEval finds the genetic dissection strongly supports interface dependence. Peer R4 confirms the niche-specific findings as a key accepted result.

Both address bacterial infiltration (C58-C59). OpenEval finds Gram staining and 16S rRNA FISH support the claims. Peer R5 confirms bacterial infiltration is demonstrated but emphasizes it is not responsible for proliferation.

Both evaluate antibiotics experiments (C60-C62). OpenEval finds the data clearly show bacteria are not required for proliferation. Peer R5 explicitly states 'Treating Cdh1 KO mice with various antibiotics did not prevent stem cell proliferation, demonstrating that bacterial infiltration is not responsible.' This is a key accepted finding.

Both address immune cell recruitment and temporal dynamics (C63-C65). OpenEval emphasizes temporal sequence showing immune cells precede bacteria. Peer R6 confirms immune recruitment findings and temporal data are accepted, with all reviewers agreeing on the sequence.

Both evaluate genetic dissection of immune recruitment (C66-C68). OpenEval finds experiments clearly demonstrate niche as source of signals. Peer R6 confirms the genetic controls and antibiotics persistence data are accepted by all reviewers.

Both address immune cell characterization (C69-C77). OpenEval finds comprehensive flow cytometry and immunofluorescence support the claims. Peer R6 confirms 'Dendritic cells (DCs) and αβ T cells, but not macrophages or γδTCR, showed marked and significant recruitment.' Reviewer 1 requests clarification on macrophage vs DC numbers but does not challenge overall findings.

Both evaluate RNA-seq analysis showing distinct transcriptional responses (C78-C82). OpenEval finds comprehensive pathway analysis supports the claims. Peer R7 confirms findings were 'revealed with RNA-Seq using FACS sorted populations.' Reviewer 1 seeks clarification on which cKO was used but does not challenge the findings. Peer R7 also covers chemokine expression (C83), which OpenEval addresses in R18.
OpenEval R18 evaluates chemokine expression and antibiotics controls (C83-C87). Peer R7 broadly accepts RNA-seq findings including chemokine data as part of the transcriptomic analysis.

Both address chemokine expression (C84-C87). OpenEval finds qRT-PCR and antibiotics controls support direct niche response. Peer R8 confirms 'Ccl1 and Ccl2, established chemokines for DCs, were the top two most highly upregulated genes.'

Both evaluate transwell migration assays and receptor blocking (C88-C94). OpenEval finds the mechanistic inference is strongly supported by receptor blocking experiments. Peer R8 confirms 'DC recruitment by HFSC is dependent on DC CCR2 expression' and notes Reviewer 2 asks follow-up questions about mechanisms, indicating interest rather than skepticism.

Both address Dex immunosuppression experiments (C95-C98). OpenEval finds data demonstrate immune cells are required for proliferation. Peer R9 expresses significant concerns: Reviewer 1 states 'experiments using dexamethasone (Dex) are quite non-specific' and requests 'specific experiments that implicate the immune cells.' While Reviewer 2 accepts the findings, specificity concerns are not fully resolved. Evaluation marked UNCERTAIN by peer reviewers.

Both evaluate Dex controls showing no direct effect on stem cells (C99-C103). OpenEval finds in vitro and bacterial persistence data support the claims. Peer R9 includes these as part of Dex experiments but maintains concerns about specificity of the approach.

Both address DC-Treg co-localization and Dex effects (C104-C106). OpenEval finds immunofluorescence supports the claims. Peer R10 notes the specificity observation but maintains concerns about Dex approach, with Reviewer 1 noting the finding is not novel (Ali et al., 2017) and genetic depletion would be more rigorous.

Both evaluate Treg co-culture proliferation assay (C107-C108). OpenEval finds the data identify Tregs as key proliferative stimulus. Peer R10 accepts the co-culture data but notes Reviewer 1 states this 'was shown recently (Ali et al., 2017) using careful genetic models,' suggesting the finding lacks novelty and the approach is less rigorous than alternatives.

Both address NOTCH pathway speculation (C109-C111). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting C111 is explicitly labeled as speculation and not directly tested. Peer R16 does not challenge the NOTCH findings, with Reviewer 1's request for 'functional analysis of BMP/FGF signaling' relating to other pathways. The speculation is accepted as interpretation rather than definitive conclusion.

Both evaluate RNA-seq showing cell cycle gene upregulation (C112-C115). OpenEval finds the experimental design appropriately dissects niche vs immune contributions. Peer R11 confirms the transcriptomic data quality, with Reviewer 1's Dex concerns relating to functional interpretation rather than the RNA-seq findings themselves.

Both address persistent immune gene expression with Dex (C116-C117). OpenEval finds the threshold model reasonable. Peer R11 does not directly challenge these transcriptomic observations, though Dex specificity concerns affect functional interpretation.

Both evaluate NFκB pathway findings (C118-C122). OpenEval finds the mechanistic model reasonable based on p120-catenin data and immunofluorescence. Peer R12 accepts the NFκB data, with Reviewer 1 asking about other transcriptional pathways, indicating interest in broader mechanisms but not challenging the NFκB findings.

OpenEval R28 synthesizes major findings (C3-C8) as supported by comprehensive evidence. Peer R13 addresses barrier sensing and niche response (C123-C130), confirming stem cells can 'sense the barrier breach' and the response is 'independent of bacterial infiltration.' Both accept the core sensing mechanism, though peer concerns about Dex relate to downstream proliferation details.

Both evaluate key conclusions about barrier breach sensing and cadherin compensation (C123-C128). OpenEval finds claims supported by bacterial infiltration and antibiotics data. Peer R13 highlights the 'fascinating observations' and confirms the breached niche response is accepted. OpenEval R29 also covers transcriptional responses (C129-C130), which peer reviewers accept as part of RNA-seq findings.

OpenEval R30 addresses distinct transcriptional responses (C129-C130) and immune recruitment capability (C133-C134). Peer R13 broadly accepts the sensing and response mechanisms as key findings, with transcriptomic data supporting these conclusions.

Both address immune recruitment as a stem cell capability (C133-C134). OpenEval finds this demonstrates a previously unrecognized function. Peer R14 calls the observations 'fascinating' and states the manuscript is 'highly novel,' accepting the conceptual framework though mechanistic details require refinement.

Both evaluate Treg proliferative effects and interpretive conclusions (C141-C147). OpenEval finds co-culture data support Tregs as key stimulus and interpretations are well-supported. Peer R14 accepts the conceptual framework as 'fascinating' and 'highly novel,' though concerns about Dex specificity affect mechanistic certainty.

Both address interpretations of barrier reinforcement efforts (C148-C151). OpenEval finds the interpretation of stem cell expansion and localized changes reasonable. Peer R15 accepts the cellular responses, with Reviewer 1 asking 'Does the proliferation that is induced in the bulge regenerate the barrier function?' seeking clarification on functional outcomes but not challenging observations. The interpretation that efforts are 'futile' in the genetic model is accepted as logical.

OpenEval R33 addresses persistent bacterial infiltration (C152) and broader implications (C153-C156). Peer R15 accepts the observed cellular responses and notes the question about barrier regeneration seeks clarification rather than challenging the data.

OpenEval R34 evaluates conclusions about immune dependence distinguishing mammalian from invertebrate systems (C157-C159). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these comparative evolutionary claims.

Both evaluate the model requiring multiple inputs for proliferation (C164-C168). OpenEval finds the mechanistic conclusion well-supported by Dex experiments showing elevated cell cycle genes are insufficient without immune signals. Peer R18 notes Dex specificity concerns relate to functional interpretation but do not challenge the transcriptomic observations. The multi-input model is logically consistent with presented data.

OpenEval R36 presents the integrated mechanistic model (C169-C174) synthesizing niche defects, immune recruitment, and proliferation specificity. No single peer review result comprehensively addresses this integrated model, though components are accepted across multiple peer results (R13, R14, R18).
